source_text: Ipsa adeo est, quae fidem et subsequitur et antecedit. denique Abraham deo credidit et iustitiae deputatus ab illo est; sed fidem eius patientia probauit, cum filium immolare iussus ad fidei, non temptationem dixerim, sed typicam contestationem, - ceterum deus quem iustitiae deputasset sciebattam graue praeceptum, quod nec domino perfici placebat, patienter et audiuit et, si deus uoluisset, implesset. merito ergo benedictus, quia et fidelis; merito fidelis, quia et patiens. ita fides patientia inluminata, cum in nationes seminaretur per semen Abrahae, quod est Christus, et gratiam legi superduceret, ampliandae adimplendaeque legi adiutricem suam patientiam praefecit, quod ea sola ad iustitiae doctrinam retro defuisset. nam olim et oculum pro oculo et dentem pro dente repetebant et malum malo fenerabant. nondum enim patientia in terris, quia nec fides. scilicet interim impatientia occasionibus legis fruebatur. facile erat absente domino patientiae et magistro. qui postquam suqeruenit et gratiam fidei patientia composuit, iam nec uerbo quidem lacessere nec \'fatue\' quidem dicere sine iudicii periculo licet. prohibita ira restricti animi, compressa petulantia manus, exemptum linguae uenenum. plus lex quam amisit inuenit. dicente Christo: diligite inimicos uestros et maledicentibus benedicite et orate pro persecutoribus uestris, ut filii sitis patris uestri caelestis. uides, quem nobis patrem patientia adquirat.
thought_title: Patience both precedes and follows faith
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that patience is inseparable from faith, proving it first from Abraham and then from Christ's new law.
pass_a_gloss: This very thing it is which both follows and precedes faith. Finally Abraham believed God and was counted to him as righteousness; but patience proved his faith, when he was ordered to sacrifice his son, for a proof of faith, I would say not a temptation, but a typical attestation, — besides, God knew what a heavy command it was, which he did not even want to be fulfilled by the Lord, he both heard it patiently and, if God had willed, he would have fulfilled it. Therefore deservedly blessed, because also faithful; deservedly faithful, because also patient. Thus faith, illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the pagans through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace in over the law, set patience as its helper before itself for the enlarging and fulfilling of the law, because this alone had been lacking for the teaching of righteousness in the past. For formerly they demanded both an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth and lent evil for evil. For patience was not yet on earth, because neither was faith. Of course in the meantime impatience was enjoying the opportunities of the law. It was easy while the Lord and teacher of patience was absent. After he came and composed grace of faith with patience, now it is not permitted even to provoke with a word nor even to say 'fool' without the danger of judgment. Anger is forbidden, the mind is restrained, wantonness of the hand is checked, the poison of the tongue is removed. The law has found more than it lost. With Christ saying: love your enemies and bless those who curse you and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be sons of your heavenly father. You see what a father patience acquires for us.

choices.why: Keeps the technical sense of 'typicus' as prefiguring Christ and 'contestatio' as a solemn proof or witness, not a mere test.

choices.english: was bringing grace in over the law
choices.why: The compound 'superduco' means to bring in upon or over; the rendering preserves the spatial metaphor of grace being laid over the law.

choices.english: for the enlarging and fulfilling of the law
choices.why: The gerundives express purpose; 'ampliare' means to enlarge or extend, distinct from 'adimplere' (fulfill), so both verbs are kept.
rejected: to expand and complete the law
for the law's increase and fulfillment

choices.why: 'Fenero' is a financial term for lending at interest; keeping 'lent' preserves the economic metaphor of repaying evil with interest.

choices.english: composed grace of faith with patience
choices.why: 'Compono' here means to put together or combine; the rendering keeps the sense that Christ joined grace, faith, and patience into one ordered whole.
rejected: arranged the grace of faith through patience
established the grace of faith with patience

choices.term: uides, quem nobis patrem patientia adquirat
choices.english: You see what a father patience acquires for us
choices.why: The exclamatory 'quem' is rendered as 'what a father' to preserve the rhetorical force of the question-like statement.
rejected: you see which father patience gains for us
you see the father patience obtains for us

pass_b_english: Patience itself is what both follows faith and goes before it. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6); but his faith was proved by patience when he was commanded to sacrifice his son—not, I would say, as a temptation of his faith, but as a typical attestation. For God, who had counted him as righteous, knew how heavy the command was, and that it was not pleasing to him to have it carried out; yet Abraham heard it patiently, and if God had willed it, he would have fulfilled it. Rightly then was he blessed, because he was also faithful; rightly faithful, because he was also patient. So faith, illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the pagans through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace in over the law, set patience before itself as its helper for the enlarging and fulfilling of the law, because patience alone had been lacking to the teaching of righteousness. For formerly they demanded an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exodus 21:24), and repaid evil for evil. Patience was not yet on the earth, because faith was not either. Meanwhile, impatience enjoyed the occasions the law provided. It was easy while the Lord and teacher of patience was absent. But after he came and composed grace of faith with patience, it is no longer permitted even to insult with a word, or even to say 'Fool,' without the danger of judgment (Matthew 5:22). Anger is forbidden, the spirit is restrained, wantonness of hand is checked, the tongue's poison is removed. The law has found more than it lost. As Christ says: Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be sons of your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:44-45). You see what a father patience acquires for us.

problems.why: Latin means 'they repaid evil with evil', not 'lent'.
problems.ruling: fenerabant means 'repaid/required interest', not 'lent'; context is retaliation, so 'lent evil for evil' misleads.

fixed: Changed 'lent evil for evil' to 'repaid evil for evil': source 'malum malo fenerabant' means they repaid evil with evil, not lent.
